title: What does Japan's GCP Ordinance require for clinical trial staff qualification and training?
seoTitle: Japan GCP Ordinance trial staff training
description: Japan's GCP Ordinance (MHW Ordinance No. 28 of 1997): investigator training, delegation lists, monitor and auditor qualification, and ICH E6(R3) status.
shortAnswer: Japan's GCP Ordinance (MHW Ordinance No. 28 of 1997) requires principal investigators to have sufficient education, training and clinical experience, sponsors to secure staff with the necessary expertise, and principal investigators to list and brief the sub-investigators and trial collaborators they delegate to. MHLW's GCP guidance adds that everyone involved must be qualified by education, training and experience, including monitors and auditors. As at November 2026, ICH E6(R3) is not yet implemented in Japan.
keyTakeaways: Article 42 of the GCP Ordinance requires a principal investigator to have received sufficient education and training to conduct the trial properly, to have sufficient clinical experience, to know the protocol and investigator's brochure, and to have enough time.
Articles 4(2) and 15-2(2) require sponsors and sponsor-investigators to secure physicians, dentists, pharmacists and others with the expertise needed for trial management.
Article 43 requires the principal investigator to prepare a list of tasks delegated to sub-investigators and trial collaborators and to explain the trial and provide the information they need.

MHLW's GCP guidance (revised July 5, 2019 to reflect ICH E6(R2)) expects monitors with appropriate training, auditors qualified by education, training and experience, and training for users of electronic data systems.
PMDA states that a Japanese translation of ICH E6(R3) will be issued as a notice; as at November 2026 the J-GCP guidance still reflects E6(R2).
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), with the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) conducting GCP compliance inspections
appliesTo: Sponsors (chiken irai-sha) of clinical trials of drugs conducted for Japanese marketing approval, and contract research organizations acting for them
Trial sites, their heads, principal investigators, sub-investigators and trial collaborators such as pharmacists, nurses and clinical research coordinators
Institutional review boards, monitors and auditors

sections.heading: What is the GCP Ordinance and when does it apply?

blocks.text: The **Ministerial Ordinance on Good Clinical Practice for Drugs** (医薬品の臨床試験の実施の基準に関する省令, MHW Ordinance No. 28 of 1997), often called J-GCP, sets the standard for clinical trials (chiken) of drugs whose results are submitted for marketing approval under the PMD Act, and for post-marketing clinical trials. Article 1 states its purpose: to protect the human rights, safety and welfare of trial subjects and to secure the scientific quality and reliability of trial results ([GCP Ordinance, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/409M50000100028)).

J-GCP was issued on March 27, 1997 to implement the original ICH E6 guideline, according to PMDA's ICH E6 page. Unlike the ICH guideline, it is a binding ministerial ordinance. MHLW's GCP guidance ("GCP Guidance") explains each article and was last substantially revised on July 5, 2019 (薬生薬審発0705第3号) to reflect ICH E6(R2) ([MHLW GCP guidance, hosted by PMDA](https://www.pmda.go.jp/files/000230974.pdf)).

Comparing e-Gov versions, the amendments in force from May 1, 2026 and the further amendments due on May 20, 2027 change Articles 1, 3, 24 and 26-10 and related provisions, but not the qualification and training articles discussed here.

sections.heading: What qualifications and training must investigators have?

blocks.text: Article 42 sets three requirements for the principal investigator (chiken sekinin ishi). The principal investigator must:

items: have received sufficient education and training to conduct the trial properly, and have sufficient clinical experience;
be thoroughly familiar with the appropriate use of the investigational product as described in the protocol, the investigator's brochure and related documents; and
have enough time to conduct the trial.

blocks.text: The GCP Guidance adds that the principal investigator must be able to conduct the trial properly through education, training and experience, must know the GCP Ordinance thoroughly and comply with it, must accept monitoring, audits and inspections with direct access to records, and should show from past results that the required number of eligible subjects can be recruited in the agreed period. Evidence of qualification takes the form of a curriculum vitae: the guidance says the principal investigator's CV submitted to the institutional review board should preferably include education, past participation in trials as an investigator or medical expert, and specialist certifications from academic societies.

sections.heading: How must tasks be delegated to sub-investigators and coordinators?

blocks.text: Through a written delegation list and a briefing. Article 43(1) requires the principal investigator, where there are sub-investigators (chiken buntan ishi) or trial collaborators (chiken kyōryokusha), to prepare a list of the tasks each is assigned. Article 43(2) requires the principal investigator to explain the trial fully to them and to give them the safety information notified by the sponsor and any other information needed to perform their delegated tasks properly.

Article 2(18) defines trial collaborators as pharmacists, nurses and other health professionals who assist the investigators under their direction, which in practice includes clinical research coordinators. The GCP Guidance describes the sponsor holding meetings with investigators and collaborators, training them and providing detailed procedures as part of preparing a trial, so the delegation list and the training record work together as evidence.

sections.heading: What do sponsors, sites and review boards need to show?

blocks.text: Each party has a staffing or competence duty. Article 4(2) requires a sponsor to secure physicians, dentists, pharmacists and others with the expertise needed to request and manage the trial, and Article 15-2(2) applies the same to sponsor-investigators. Article 35 requires a trial site to have the facilities and staff for adequate clinical observation and testing, to be able to take emergency measures, and to have sufficient investigators, pharmacists, nurses and other staff. Article 36 requires the head of the site to prepare procedures for trial work, and Article 38 requires the head to appoint a trial secretariat.

For institutional review boards, Article 28 requires at least five members, including a member without medical or clinical trial expertise and members independent of the site and of the board's founder, with written procedures and a published member list.

blocks.text: Not yet. PMDA's ICH E6 page lists the E6(R3) Step 4 guideline and states that its Japanese translation will be issued as a notice or administrative communication in future, while the implemented (Step 5) materials listed for Japan are the E6(R2) documents of July 5, 2019, including the revised GCP Guidance, basic principles on quality management in trials and on risk-based monitoring ([PMDA ICH E6 page](https://www.pmda.go.jp/int-activities/int-harmony/ich/0028.html)). PMDA does publish ICH's E6(R3) training modules on that page.

As at November 2026, Japanese sites and sponsors therefore work to the GCP Ordinance and the 2019 guidance, while global sponsors may already apply E6(R3) under EU or US expectations. The training expectations of E6(R3), including role-proportionate training rather than blanket repetition, are covered in [ICH E6(R3) GCP training requirements](/regulations/ich-e6-r3-gcp-training-requirements). Training programs serving both should map each topic to its J-GCP article and to the E6(R3) section.

sections.heading: How long must trial records, including training evidence, be kept?

blocks.text: Article 41 requires the head of the trial site to appoint a records custodian, who must keep source documents, contracts, consent forms, documents prepared under the ordinance, documents received from the review board and records of trial work until the later of the date the product is approved (or three years after notice that development has stopped) and three years after the trial ends or is discontinued. Investigator CVs, delegation lists and training records are part of the trial records the site and sponsor are expected to retain; see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps J-GCP articles, the MHLW GCP Guidance and the ICH E6(R3) sections as parallel obligations, so one training design can show coverage of both. Role-based learning outcomes and assessment points are defined before content, and protocol amendments trigger targeted retraining records against the affected roles.

faqs.q: Does J-GCP require GCP certification for investigators?
faqs.a: No specific certificate is required. Article 42 requires sufficient education, training and clinical experience, and the GCP Guidance expects these to be shown through a curriculum vitae that preferably includes trial history and specialist certifications. Sponsors and sites commonly use GCP course records as part of that evidence.

faqs.q: How often must clinical trial staff in Japan repeat GCP training?
faqs.a: Neither the GCP Ordinance nor the 2019 GCP Guidance sets a refresher interval. Training is tied to the trial: protocol, product and procedure training before the work and on changes. Sponsors and sites set general GCP refresher periods in their own procedures.

faqs.q: Who counts as a trial collaborator under J-GCP?
faqs.a: Article 2(18) defines trial collaborators as pharmacists, nurses and other health professionals who assist the principal investigator or sub-investigators with trial work under their direction. Clinical research coordinators typically fall in this group and must appear on the Article 43 delegation list.

faqs.q: Can a Japanese site follow ICH E6(R3) now?
faqs.a: A site can adopt E6(R3) practices where they are consistent with the GCP Ordinance, which remains binding. As at November 2026, PMDA lists E6(R3) as Step 4 with a Japanese notice still to be issued, so the 2019 GCP Guidance based on E6(R2) is the official interpretation.
